trigger: gtest EXPECT at AsyncSSLSocketTest.cpp:3797 (byteEvents size 3 < 4) and :3812 (ACK max offset missing) after the first writeAndReflect
originating_invariant: writeAndReflect assumes that once the reflected byte has been read, all byte events for the write (including the ACK) have been handed to the observer. This holds only if no other server-to-client data (TLS 1.3 NewSessionTickets) is pending when the timestamped write is made, because AsyncSocket drains the error queue only at ioReady entry, not between reads in handleRead.

hypotheses.claim: Test synchronization race: the server's TLS 1.3 post-handshake NewSessionTicket records are still unread when the first timestamped write is issued. The client is inside AsyncSocket::handleRead consuming the tickets when the server's echo, carrying the TCP ACK, arrives. handleRead keeps looping and reads the echo without re-draining the socket error queue, where the ACK timestamp is already queued, so writeAndReflect returns before the ACK ByteEvent is delivered to the observer.
hypotheses.supporting: (a) FAIL has exactly WRITE/SCHED/TX (3 events) and no ACK for offset 501; the second block, which requires >= startNum+4 and ACK == new offset, passes, so the ACK is late, not lost. (b) Guest stderr ordering: in FAIL the server handshake completes (tickets sent) before the client's first write; in PASS it completes after. (c) The hermit syscall trace of the seed-11 replay (witness/syscalls-fd16-fd17-prefix-fail-1.txt) shows server tickets #90/#102 (239 B each) sent before client sendmsg #3151 (23 B timestamped). The client drains 2 errqueue messages (#3162, #3164, flag 8192=MSG_ERRQUEUE), then at ioReady entry the errqueue is empty (#3171). handleRead reads ticket1 (#3172-3173) and ticket2 (#3176-3177); the server echoes (#119); the client reads the echo (#3179-3180) in the same loop with no errqueue recvmsg in between. After write 2 the errqueue yields 3 messages (#3198/#3200/#3202), which is the late ACK plus SCHED and TX. In PASS the tickets carry the ACK and it is drained (#3159-#3165) before any read. (d) AsyncSocket::ioReady calls handleErrMessages only on entry, and handleRead loops up to maxReadsPerEvent_ reads. (e) The sibling test ObserverAttachedAfterConnect documents this exact sequence and mitigates it with serverHandshakeCb_->waitForHandshake() plus an untimestamped writeAndReflect.
hypotheses.contradicting: No post-fix run of seed 11 exists, because the investigator cannot build. The claim that the ACK timestamp is enqueued at the server's echo sendmsg (#119) is inferred from kernel TCP semantics (tcp_ack runs before the payload is queued), not directly observed; the trace records only userspace syscalls.
hypotheses.next_experiment: Controller: build the patched ELF, replay sched-seed 11 (expect PASS) and seed 1 (expect PASS), and run fresh seeds 12-15. In the post-fix trace, the timestamped write's echo should be preceded by an errqueue recvmsg returning the ACK, and no ticket reads should follow the timestamped sendmsg.

hypotheses.claim: The ACK timestamp had not been generated by the kernel when the echo was read, for example because of delayed ACK on the server with the echo not carrying the ACK.
hypotheses.supporting: ACK is the only missing event type, and it depends on peer behavior.
hypotheses.contradicting: A TCP data segment from the server necessarily acknowledges all client bytes the server has received. The server read the 'a' record before echoing it, so the echo segment acknowledges offset 501, and the kernel processes the ACK (and queues the TX_ACK timestamp) before queueing the payload. The FAIL trace shows 3 errqueue messages after write 2, consistent with a queued but unread ACK rather than a missing one.
hypotheses.next_experiment: Instrument (or trace in hermit) an extra recvmsg(MSG_ERRQUEUE) immediately after the echo read in the FAIL schedule. H2 predicts EAGAIN; H1 predicts the ACK timestamp for offset 501.

hypotheses.claim: Production defect in AsyncSocket: ioReady/handleRead should drain the error queue between reads (or re-check it after handleRead), so ByteEvent delivery ordering relative to readDataAvailable is wrong.
hypotheses.supporting: It is the same mechanism: handleRead consumes data that arrived after an already-queued ACK timestamp, and the ACK is surfaced only on the next ioReady.
hypotheses.contradicting: The event is not lost. EPOLLERR is level-triggered, and it is delivered on the next loop iteration, which is within folly's documented contract (no ordering guarantee between ByteEvents and reads). The maintainers already chose a test-side mitigation for the identical sequence in ObserverAttachedAfterConnect. Changing the hot read path would add a syscall per read iteration for all sockets.
hypotheses.next_experiment: Prototype handleErrMessages() inside the handleRead loop, replay seed 11 without the test change, and measure the per-read syscall overhead. Treat it as a separate design discussion, not a flake fix.

hypotheses.claim: Hermit artifact: ptrace/chaos scheduling or epoll emulation hides EPOLLERR, or produces a kernel interleaving that cannot occur natively.
hypotheses.supporting: The failure appears under hermit chaos scheduling with a specific seed.
hypotheses.contradicting: The interleaving (server tickets and echo interleaved with client reads) is legal on native loopback. The sibling test's comment states that the same sequence made that test flaky outside hermit. The trace shows real errqueue reads returning the late ACK after write 2, so EPOLLERR is not being hidden.
hypotheses.next_experiment: Run the unpatched test natively under CPU contention (stress or taskset on a single core) and look for the same missing-ACK failure.
